Depends on how you mean.

  • Many polyamorous people are in committed monogamous relationships. Just because they'd be OK with poly themselves doesn't mean they're going to drag an unwilling partner into it. In this sense, yes it's a choice because poly folks can be in monogamous relationships.

  • Many people have polyamorous partners and don't feel poly themselves. They may go along with the relationship anyway - you can be the judge of how healthy that is. In this sense, yes it's a choice because non-poly folks can choose to live in poly lifestyles.

  • Finally, many polyamorous people consider poly as part of their identity. Even if they're in a monogamous relationship, being poly is part of who they are. They may be unable or unwilling to consider themselves monogamous. In this sense, no it's not a choice. Even if they're not acting on it, a poly person may consider being poly part of their identity.

To be fair, the title is somewhat sensationalized. Sure CRISPR could change a species forever, but we could also use other cloning approaches to restore the original genotype.

Not to mention that this is how evolution has worked for a few billion years now. CRISPR knocks out genes the same way evolution has through other silencing mechanisms. Throughout the course of evolution a species can have genes that are lost, duplicated, or gained. Sometimes, duplicated genes slowly mutate, creating two distinct genes with overlapping or disparate functions.

Genes have also been transferred from one organism to another many times. Horizontal gene transfer is well documented:

Plant to animal gene transferred has been documented.

Humans are thought to have over a hundred genes from other organisms.

Animal-to-plant DNA transfer has been observed in pine trees, spruces, and other conifers.

Agrobacteria have inserted several transgenes into the sweet potato genome about 8,000 years ago.
